# The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter, for clinical readers

URL: https://furkanbekdemir.com/notes/hierarchical-gaussian-filter

You are reading a computational psychiatry paper. There is a model name, a few
Greek letters, and a sentence saying some parameter was higher in the patient
group. This note is about what that sentence claims, and more usefully, what it
does not.

No equations. The aim is not to let you build the model but to know where to
look when someone else's model produces a claim. For the mathematics and working
code, [Perception, Beliefs, and the Hierarchical Gaussian
Filter](https://metaduck.com/computational-psychiatry-afterburn-hierarchical-gaussian-filters/)
builds it step by step with `pyhgf`.

## The problem it solves
Suppose you watch a patient learn something. Say they are working out which of
two boxes pays out more often. What you have is a sequence of trial-by-trial
answers: A on this one, B on the next, then A again.

What can you read off that sequence? At the simplest you count how often they
were right. That number says nothing about how the learning happened. Two
patients can score identically having taken completely different routes: one
revised on every new piece of evidence, the other held out and then switched all
at once.

The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter assumes there is a person behind the sequence
and describes how that person learns with a handful of numbers. What it models
is not the behaviour but the process producing it.

## What the hierarchy means
The "hierarchical" in the name refers to layers of uncertainty stacked on one
another.

The bottom layer is the current state: is this box paying out right now. Above
it sits the tendency: how often does this box pay out in general. The top layer
is how changeable the world is, meaning how often those rules shift.

That third layer is the model's real idea and the one with the most clinical
purchase. How fast you ought to learn depends on how much the world actually
changes. If the rules shift often, revising quickly is sensible. If they are
fixed, the same speed has you chasing noise.

People make this adjustment constantly and the model puts a number on it.
Someone who takes the world to be more volatile than it is treats a single event
as too informative. Someone who takes the opposite view is slow to notice a real
change.

## What the parameters say clinically
The number reported most often is the learning rate, and the HGF's difference is
that the rate is not fixed. In classical learning models a person has one
learning speed and it stays the same from trial to trial. Here it is recomputed
on every trial, and it depends on how certain the person is at that moment and
how volatile they take the world to be. Learning speeds up after a surprise and
slows inside a familiar pattern.

The quantity governing this is precision. It has nothing to do with precision in
the everyday sense; it measures how narrow a belief is. A narrow belief leaves
little room for new evidence, a wide one leaves a lot. That is the clinically
interesting part: the source of a symptom may not be the evidence but the weight
given to it.

The engine is prediction error, the gap between what happened and what was
expected. The raw gap is not what gets used; the precision-weighted version is.
A surprise of the same size produces a different result depending on how certain
the person was.

There is also response noise, which absorbs everything the model cannot explain.
People do not always act on their beliefs; they get distracted, press the wrong
key, waver. Having this parameter matters, because without it disorderly
behaviour would look like a strange style of learning.

The appeal of these numbers is obvious. Each resembles a mechanism and attaches
easily to a clinical story. The two sections below are largely against that
ease.

## Why model comparison is not optional
A model was fitted and numbers came out. For those numbers to mean anything you
first have to know whether this model generated the data, or whether some other
model would have generated it just as well.

Goodness of fit does not answer that. A flexible enough model fits any data
well, and a good fit may be showing you flexibility rather than truth.

So fitting one model and reporting its numbers is not enough. Several candidate
models are built, all fitted to the same data, and compared on how well each
explains it. Because the comparison separately penalises complex models, adding
parameters to improve the fit does not count as winning.

If a paper has no model comparison, the parameters it reports do not point at a
mechanism. They are what you get when you summarise the data through that
particular model. The difference is not a small one.

## When to trust a finding
When a model fits, it produces a number for every parameter. That a number was
produced does not mean the data carried information about that parameter. In
some models two parameters move together: raise one and lower the other and the
model behaves identically. Their combination can then be read off the data but
neither can be read alone. The estimator still returns a number, because it has
to. That number reflects setup choices more than it reflects data.

The technical name for this is identifiability. It is among the first things to
ask about a computational finding.

The test is parameter recovery. You generate synthetic data from known values,
run the same pipeline over it, and check whether the values you put in come back
out. If they do not, the parameter cannot be measured with that design, and
there is no way to discover this from real data. I ran this on my own pipeline
before collecting anything, and I think the order matters: leave it until
afterwards and, when the result is bad, you are holding a number you could
publish, which makes it harder to drop.

Finally, parameter names. Calling a parameter "belief instability" or "learning
flexibility" does not establish that it measures that. The name is the
interpretation of whoever built the model. The same number can be attached to a
completely different mechanism under another reading, and choosing between the
two takes more than the model.

## In short
The HGF's clinical value is that it treats learning speed as an adjustment
tracking how volatile a person takes the world to be, rather than as a fixed
trait.

But not every number it produces is a mechanism. The estimator returns a number
under any conditions; what shows the number measures something is not the number
itself but the model comparison and the recovery behind it. Without both, what
you are holding is a summary statistic rather than a claim about mechanism. And
if the parameter's name is confident enough, that summary statistic gets read as
a mechanism.

The model itself:

Mathys C, Daunizeau J, Friston KJ, Stephan KE. A Bayesian foundation for
individual learning under uncertainty. *Frontiers in Human Neuroscience*.
2011;5:39. doi:[10.3389/fnhum.2011.00039](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00039)

Mathys CD, Lomakina EI, Daunizeau J, Iglesias S, Brodersen KH, Friston KJ,
Stephan KE. Uncertainty in perception and the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter.
*Frontiers in Human Neuroscience*.
2014;8:825. doi:[10.3389/fnhum.2014.00825](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00825)

Model comparison and parameter recovery:

# Sensory attenuation and the force-matching task

URL: https://furkanbekdemir.com/notes/sensory-attenuation

You cannot tickle yourself. There is a measurable mechanism behind that familiar
observation, and where it weakens, psychiatric symptoms appear.

Tickling is only its most familiar form. The same mechanism has a laboratory
measure, and that measure connects to several separate symptoms. The precision
language used here is set out in the [HGF
note](hierarchical-gaussian-filter.qmd); the rig I built for the task is on the
[instrument page](../tools/force-matching.qmd).

## The observation
Touching your own palm and having someone else touch it the same way differ in
nothing physical. Same pressure, same skin, same receptors. The only thing that
changes is where the touch came from, and that is what drops the perceived
intensity.

Blakemore and colleagues looked at this in 1998. Somatosensory cortex was more
active for externally produced touch and less active for self-produced touch. In
the cerebellum the pattern reversed: cerebellar activity was lower for movements
that produced a touch than for movements that did not. The reading is that the
cerebellum computes the sensory consequence of a movement in advance, and that
computation is used to turn the incoming signal down.

The name for that turning down is sensory attenuation. Its use is this: most of
the signal reaching your senses is produced by your own movements. If all of it
were processed at equal weight, the externally caused signal, the one that
actually carries news, would be lost inside it. Turning down the predictable is
how you bring out the unpredictable.

## How the task turns it into a number
The most memorable demonstration involved two people. In 2003 Shergill and
colleagues had participants take turns pressing on each other's finger, each
trying to apply the force they had just felt. The force grew every turn. Nobody
was exaggerating; everyone matched what they felt, but because they felt their
own output as weaker than it was, each put in a little more. The paper's title
sums it up as two eyes for an eye. So the line we all used as children, that he
hit first and he hit harder, was not a lie after all. It was a calibration
problem.

The same effect was turned into a standard single-person task. In the
force-matching task a target force is applied to the participant's finger and
they are then asked to reproduce it two ways. In the direct condition they press
on their own finger with the other hand. In the slider condition a motor
produces the force and they set its size with a slider.

Pressing directly, they overshoot. Through the slider they are fairly accurate.
In the twenty-five-participant data published in McNaughton's device paper the
direct condition ran 0.50 N high on average and the slider condition 0.30 N low.
The difference between the two conditions is the measurement.

## The second condition is not decoration
Why the slider condition is needed is not obvious at first, and misreading the
task usually starts here.

Error in the direct condition has more than one source. You have to remember the
target force, you have to scale the force you produce, and your motor output has
noise of its own. None of that is specific to prediction, and each would produce
a deviation on its own. The slider condition carries the same memory and scaling
load, but because the force does not come from your own hand, prediction-based
attenuation is not running. Take the difference between the two and the shared
effects drop out, leaving the part that belongs to prediction.

That logic was recently tested formally. Valè and colleagues built a
computational model of the task on data from nearly five hundred participants,
separated the individual noise sources including memory noise, and showed that
the difference between conditions does isolate the predictive component. Two
further things came out of the same study. Attenuated sensations vary more from
trial to trial, because they carry the noise of the prediction as well. And
attenuation works by division rather than subtraction: the signal is not reduced
by a fixed amount, it shrinks by a factor.

What attenuation locks onto has been tested too. Bays and colleagues showed the
mechanism attaches not to the movement but to the event the movement predicts.
Shift the timing of the touch earlier or later and attenuation falls off.
Movements that stop above the finger or pass wide of it produce no attenuation
at all. The system is not saying "I am moving, turn the senses down." It is
saying "a touch is about to happen, there, now." Kilteni and Ehrsson showed a
more basic condition still: you have to count the touching hand as your own.
Move the sense of ownership with the rubber hand illusion and attenuation moves
with it.

## The link to precision
In active inference, attenuation corresponds to lowering the precision of
sensory evidence during movement. The argument that this is compulsory runs as
follows: to move, your prediction that you are moving has to outweigh the
sensory evidence that you are not yet moving. If that evidence is not
down-weighted, the movement never starts.

Brown and colleagues reproduced the force-matching finding from this framework.
When they took attenuation out of the model two things happened together: the
overshoot in the task disappeared, and false inferences about agency appeared.
The same setting makes movement possible and determines what counts as yours. It
costs in both directions. Turn it down too little and movement does not start;
too much and you cannot tell yourself from the world.

## Where it sits clinically
The most instructive finding is one of the oldest. In 2000 Blakemore and
colleagues compared patients with schizophrenia, patients with bipolar disorder
or depression, and healthy controls. What determined the loss of attenuation was
the symptom rather than the diagnosis: attenuation was absent in those with
auditory hallucinations or passivity experiences and present in those without,
regardless of what they were diagnosed with.

What followed widened it. Attenuation was shown to be significantly reduced in
schizophrenia, and in an imaging study the loss of attenuation in secondary
somatosensory cortex was predicted by the patient's current hallucination
severity. Teufel and colleagues worked in healthy people: those higher in
delusional ideation were more accurate on the task, meaning they attenuated
less. That last one answers two objections at once, since neither medication nor
an active episode can explain it.

Leaving the picture in schizophrenia would be a mistake. In functional movement
disorder attenuation is absent; patients do not experience the movement as under
their own control and do not produce the overshoot that controls produce. In
Parkinson's disease attenuation is selectively impaired in the group reporting
fatigue and not in the group without it, and the impairment goes with subjective
fatigue and perceived effort rather than motor symptom severity. In chronic pain
no group difference in magnitude was found; what separated the groups was
variance.

Attenuation being disturbed across this many presentations makes it a measure
tied to symptoms rather than diagnoses. It does not tell you which diagnosis a
patient carries. It says something about which mechanism is disturbed. Confuse
the two and the measure has promised more than it can deliver.

## What the instrument contributes
Because the measurement is a difference between two conditions, instrument error
common to both cancels in that difference. What does not cancel is error that
depends on the direction of loading, since the two conditions do not load the
sensor the same way. A ramp pressed by a motor and a ramp pressed by a person
are not the same thing.

The acceptance criterion that passed by the narrowest margin on my own rig was
hysteresis. That is no coincidence: hysteresis is exactly the class of error
that does not cancel in the difference. The rig and its calibration record are
on the [instrument page](../tools/force-matching.qmd).

## Reading a finding
The first thing to look at in a published attenuation result is how many
conditions the design had. A deviation coming out of a single-condition design
cannot be called attenuation, because the second condition is what strips memory
and scaling back out.

Next come the number of repetitions and the time window. McNaughton and
colleagues showed in data from a hundred and thirty-eight participants that the
number of repetitions can come down from eight, that the best window for
extracting the matched force is 2.5 to 3.0 seconds, and that performance does
not drift over the session. Where the window is not reported there is no ground
for comparing two studies.

Last, whether the analysis looked only at the mean. In chronic pain the groups
did not separate on magnitude but did on variance, and an analysis of means
would never see a difference like that. Given that Valè and colleagues' model
says variability may be predictive signal rather than noise, this is no longer a
secondary detail.
